Lưu Sắc Kim Hoàng là chiến dịch truyền t: Lưu Sắc Kim Hoàng is a cultural communications campaign honoring the revival of Kim Hoàng folk paintings — a traditional art form deeply rooted in Hà Nội's artistic and cultural heritage.
Ra đời vào nửa sau thế kỷ XVIII tại làng: Originating in the second half of the 18th century in Kim Hoàng village, Hoài Đức, Hà Nội, Kim Hoàng paintings were renowned for their signature vermilion-red paper, delicate woodblock carvings, and expressive color palette. Yet amid historical upheavals and the passage of time, this folk tradition nearly faded into oblivion.
Từ câu chuyện ấy, Lưu Sắc Kim Hoàng ra đ: Born from that story, Lưu Sắc Kim Hoàng sets out to chronicle the revival journey while recognizing and honoring the artisans, researchers, and individuals who devoted themselves to safeguarding Kim Hoàng art. Through storytelling, exhibitions, and hands-on experiences, the campaign invites the public to discover the beauty of Kim Hoàng paintings and rekindle a lasting love for traditional Vietnamese folk art.
Góp phần đưa tranh dân gian Kim Hoàng đế: Bringing Kim Hoàng folk paintings closer to the public; serving as a bridge between heritage custodians and folk art enthusiasts, fostering appreciation, contemporary creativity, and the continuity of Kim Hoàng artistic values in modern life.
Lan tỏa câu chuyện về quá trình khôi phụ: Share the story of restoring Kim Hoàng folk paintings and the timeless artistic values preserved across generations.
Bày tỏ sự trân trọng và biết ơn đến các: Pay tribute to the artisans, researchers, and dedicated individuals who poured their hearts and efforts into reviving and preserving this craft.
Tạo cơ hội để mọi người tìm hiểu, khám p: Create opportunities for everyone to learn, explore, and directly experience the art of Kim Hoàng folk painting.
Khơi dậy tình yêu đối với nghệ thuật tru: Inspire a love for traditional art and encourage younger generations to care for, preserve, and share Kim Hoàng heritage in contemporary life.

trân trọng giới thiệu Tiến sĩ Nguyễn Thị: proudly introduces Dr. Nguyễn Thị Thu Hòa — Director of the Hà Nội Ceramic Museum, who has made pivotal contributions to researching and reviving Kim Hoàng folk paintings.
Với nhiều năm nghiên cứu và sưu tầm mỹ t: With decades of researching and collecting Vietnamese folk art, Dr. Thu Hòa initiated the Kim Hoàng revival project in 2015. From surviving archives and traces, she brought together scholars, artisans, and painters to verify and restore a nearly lost artistic heritage.
Hành trình ấy không đơn thuần là làm lại: The journey went far beyond recreating lost prints. It involved researching surviving archives and artifacts, studying forms, pigments, paper, and techniques, and uniting specialists to restore motifs, woodblocks, and hand-coloring methods — yielding 33 woodblock prints and 19 hand-painted works while passing the craft on to local residents.
Bên cạnh hành trình phục hồi tranh Kim H: Alongside the Kim Hoàng revival, Dr. Nguyễn Thị Thu Hòa has dedicated herself to documenting and introducing Vietnam's folk painting traditions through scholarly publications, systematizing archives and deepening public appreciation of their artistic, cultural, and historical significance.

Nguồn Cội Phường Tranh Kim Hoàng: Origins of the Kim Hoàng Painting Guild
Kim Hoàng là một làng ven đô, phía tây t: Kim Hoàng was a village on the outskirts of the ancient city of Thăng Long, to its west (now part of Sơn Đồng Commune, Hà Nội). According to the book Đồ Họa Co Việt Nam (Ancient Vietnamese Graphics), in the 22nd year of the Chính Hòa reign (1701), the people of Kim Bảng and Hoàng Bảng villages migrated from Thanh Hóa to the North and merged to form Kim Hoàng village.
Theo đó, nhận thấy tranh Đông Hồ chỉ đủ: Recognizing that Đông Hồ paintings could only meet the demand in areas such as Hà Bắc, Hải Dương and Nam Định; Hàng Trống paintings primarily served Hà Nội and were unsuitable for farmers in terms of both aesthetics and affordability, the people of Kim Hoàng, led by the Nguyễn Sỹ and Nguyễn Thế families, set out to create a new genre of folk painting that combined the techniques of both Đông Hồ and Hàng Trống. Gradually, the production of Kim Hoàng paintings was organized into a “painting guild”, drawing the entire village into the trade.
Hàng năm vào rằm tháng Giêng, người làng: Every year, on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, the people of Kim Hoàng began their annual painting season. The paintings were produced using woodblocks. These blocks were kept by the guild master, who was skilled in both drawing and carving. During the printing process, families exchanged woodblocks with one another. At the end of the season, all the blocks were returned to the guild master.
Vào những ngày giáp Tết xưa, không khí l: In the days leading up to Tết, the village was once filled with the bustling atmosphere of painting production. Everyone worked tirelessly throughout the day and night, and when evening came, they would light oil lamps to apply colours to the prints. After nearly a year of preparation, around the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month, the paintings were taken to markets in the surrounding areas for sale. Early in the morning, each painting-making household would send someone to the local markets to “reserve a spot with a stick”. Only when daylight broke would other family members carry bundles of paintings to set up their stalls and sell them individually to local people preparing for the Lunar New Year. Kim Hoàng paintings were carried to markets such as Sấu Giá, Son Đong, Chùa Thầy, Canh and Dien. According to the recollections of the village elders, in prosperous years, a person returning from the market after selling paintings would carry a shoulder pole heavily laden with Tự Đức copper coins.
Cụ Trần Sơn Phương lại có những ký ức ri: Elder Trần Sơn Phương, however, had his own distinct memories of the painting trade in Kim Hoàng: “My father made a living as a painting merchant. Every Tết, he would go to collect paintings and sell them throughout the surrounding areas. Regularly, as evening fell, he would visit familiar suppliers to collect the paintings, tie them securely into bundles, and then set off early the next morning to sell them at markets in the area. Back then, trading was simple, yet full of joy. Kim Hoàng paintings were an indispensable item in every household during Tết, so whatever quantity my father collected each day, he would sell out by the end of that day. When he returned home in the afternoon, the load on his shoulders was almost weightless. My siblings and I would run after him excitedly, begging him to let us hang from the carrying pole's ropes…”
Tết Hà Nội 1896, chụp bởi Andres Salles: Hà Nội Tết 1896, photographed by Andres Salles
Đến năm Ất Mão đời Duy Tân (1915), xảy r: In the year Ất Mão, during the reign of Duy Tân (1915), a major flood occurred when the Liên Mạc dike broke, inundating a vast area west of Hà Nội and sweeping away the woodblock storage of the Kim Hoàng painting guild. From then on, the Kim Hoàng painting trade began to decline. Only a handful of households remained, reluctant to part with their painting blocks, and tried to preserve them in order to keep the craft alive.
Thêm vào đó, về sau thị hiếu người dân c: In addition, as people's tastes gradually shifted towards Hàng Trống paintings, the people of Kim Hoàng began purchasing Hàng Trống paintings to resell in the surrounding rural villages. As a result, the market for Kim Hoàng paintings gradually shrank. At first, a few households in Kim Hoàng still tried to hold on to the trade, driven by hope and lingering attachment to the craft.
Đến năm 1945 khi cuộc chiến chống Pháp b: By 1945, when the resistance war against the French began, the impact of war, famine and increasingly difficult living conditions forced the remaining woodblocks to be sold. The custom of displaying folk paintings during Tết also gradually faded over time, causing the village's printing trade to fall apart. “By around the late 1950s, the campaign against superstitious practices led to the remaining woodblocks being chopped up for firewood,” recalled Trần Ất, the oldest person in the village. And so, Kim Hoàng lost an entire genre of folk painting…
Tư liệu TTXVN, tổng hợp bởi báo Nhân Dân: VNA Archive, compiled by Báo Nhân Dân
Tưởng chừng số phận dòng tranh Kim Hoàng: It seemed that the fate of the Kim Hoàng painting tradition had been forgotten. However, the French researcher Maurice Durand had collected ancestral worship paintings and Tết paintings from Northern Vietnam and preserved them at the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient (EFEO), among which were several original Kim Hoàng paintings. In 1960, Maurice Durand's book Tranh dan gian Việt Nam (L'imagerie populaire Vietnamienne) was published. Besides the two famous painting traditions of Hàng Trống and Đông Hồ, Durand also introduced several other paintings without specifying their origins. It was only after many years of searching that the Vietnam Fine Arts Museum eventually traced these paintings back to Kim Hoàng village, right at the gateway to the capital city of Hà Nội.
Các cụ cao tuổi ở làng Kim Hoàng khi xem: When the elderly villagers of Kim Hoàng looked through M. Durand's book, they too recognized the familiar paintings of their village. Although these were only black-and-white photographs, they seemed to evoke the hues of the red paintings of years gone by. And so, the Kim Hoàng folk painting tradition officially entered the history of fine arts research in Vietnam.
Đến năm 2011, sự may mắn đã đến với công: In 2011, a stroke of good fortune came to the efforts to collect and restore Kim Hoàng paintings when the French School of the Far East (EFEO) republished Tranh dan gian Việt Nam, this time featuring colour illustrations of folk paintings. Based on examinations of colours, lines and artistic styles, researchers identified 58 Kim Hoàng folk paintings among them. This became an important source of reference, opening up possibilities for researching and reconstructing the Kim Hoàng painting tradition with its distinctive red background.
Đến khoảng năm 2013, hai cụ cao niên làn: Around 2013, two elderly villagers from Kim Hoàng travelled to Đông Hồ painting village to seek assistance in restoring the woodblocks, but their efforts were unsuccessful.

Không cam tâm để dòng tranh này chỉ còn: Unwilling to accept that this painting tradition should exist only in a few brief lines on the pages of books, antique art collector Nguyễn Thị Thu Hòa (Director of the Bảo tàng Hà Nội of Ceramics) travelled to Kim Hoàng village to speak with its elderly residents. In 2015, Dr. Nguyễn Thị Thu Hòa officially initiated a project to revive Kim Hoàng folk paintings. She was determined to restore the Kim Hoàng folk painting tradition and bring it back into contemporary life. “But of course, it sounds wonderful when put into words, but the work is extremely difficult and exhausting.” To revive a painting tradition that had been lost, historical documents alone were not enough. It also required research into printing techniques, colours, paper materials, painting methods, as well as the involvement of artisans knowledgeable in Vietnamese folk painting and artists experienced in woodblock printing.
Ý thức được hành trình gian nan phía trư: Aware of the arduous journey ahead, Thu Hòa proactively sought out and brought together a team of leading experts, researchers and artisans to work towards this common goal. She shared: “To revive this painting tradition, we needed a very large team working alongside one another. This is because the work does not stop at tracing its origins; it also requires the meticulous reconstruction of every stage of the process: from researching colours and paper materials, to printing methods, colouring techniques and even the techniques used to dry the paintings.”

Dự án nhanh chóng nhận được sự chung tay: The project quickly received the support and contributions of many renowned researchers and artisans. While researcher Trần Hậu Yên Thế and calligrapher Lê Quốc Việt compared historical materials to restore the distinctive artistic characteristics of the paintings, traditional artisans contributed their expertise in technical aspects: artisan Nguyễn Đăng Chế (Đông Hồ) shared his knowledge of paper dyeing, artisan Nguyễn Đăng Tâm (Đông Hồ) took part in woodblock carving, and artisan Lê Đình Nghiên (Hàng Trống) provided guidance on traditional hand-colouring techniques. The responsibility for recreating and expanding the range of painting designs was entrusted to two artists, Nguyễn Đức Hòa and Đức Phương. Together, they brought exemplary paintings such as Than ke and Lon doc back to life through woodblock carving, painting and printing techniques that created raised forms. In particular, alongside restoring the traditional designs, artist Nguyễn Đức Hòa also created new painting designs that inherited the artistic essence of Kim Hoàng, breathing new life into the painting tradition in contemporary society.
Bước đầu, để xác định màu tranh được sử: At the initial stage, even determining the colours used in the paintings proved to be a challenging process. Based on Maurice Durand's book, the research team identified the colours as orange-red and canary yellow. However, as the colours in the collection may have faded over time, artist Nguyễn Đức Hòa experimented with mixing different shades of orange. On the other hand, according to documents by various previous researchers, Kim Hoàng folk paintings were printed on a type of paper known as "tau vang", although its exact nature has yet to be identified. The researchers hypothesized that, in order to keep production costs low and make the paintings accessible to the wider population, particularly farming households, the materials used to produce the colours may have been sourced from common materials readily available in the local area, such as the writing paper used by scholars of old.

Công việc không dừng ở việc làm ra những: The work did not stop at producing paintings that closely resembled the original designs. The woodblocks had to be restored or recreated; the printed lines needed to retain their original character; the colours had to reflect the distinctive characteristics of the painting tradition; and the colouring techniques needed to be flexible enough for each work to retain its own individual nuances. It was a process that involved research, practice and verification, in which knowledge drawn from historical materials had to be translated into the practical skills of the artisans.
Từ nỗ lực ấy, những mẫu tranh Kim Hoàng: Through these efforts, Kim Hoàng painting designs gradually returned. The project successfully restored 33 woodblock-printed designs and 19 hand-painted designs. These figures demonstrate the tangible results of the restoration process, while also providing a foundation for further research, introduction and practice of the painting tradition in contemporary life.
Một dòng tranh chỉ thực sự có cơ hội sốn: A painting tradition can only truly have a chance of surviving when there are people who master its techniques, have the means to practise the craft and find economic and cultural value in their work. Therefore, rather than simply restoring paintings for preservation in museums, the project aimed to pass on these skills to local people. Artisan Đào Đình Chung, a resident of Kim Hoàng village, was supported in learning the various stages of woodblock carving, colour mixing, printing and painting completion. Since 2019, he has been able to make a living independently from the Kim Hoàng painting trade, without requiring further financial support from the project. This is a noteworthy sign: conservation efforts have begun to create livelihoods, enabling those who practise traditional culture to continue their craft through their own abilities.
Phần 7 • Sức Sống Mới Của Tranh Dân Gian: Part 7 • New Vitality of Kim Hoàng Folk Paintings in Contemporary Life
Tính đến nay đã gần 10 năm kể từ khi tra: Nearly ten years have now passed since Kim Hoàng paintings were officially revived. Although the project has come to an end, the Kim Hoàng folk painting tradition continues to develop. Artisan Chung remains dedicated to painting, while also actively participating in communications activities to promote this folk painting tradition and help it reach a wider audience. Alongside the traditional designs painted by artisans, young people today are also actively incorporating Kim Hoàng folk paintings into modern materials and applications that are highly practical and more accessible in contemporary life. From technology and fashion to education, Kim Hoàng folk paintings are now being adapted in flexible and creative ways to make them more vivid and relevant, while still preserving their original qualities and distinctive characteristics.
Có thể thấy rằng, để viết lại lịch sử là: It is clear that rewriting history has never been an easy task. Through exploration, research, experimentation and development, the people involved in the journey to revive Kim Hoàng folk paintings have devoted immense passion, dedication, effort, time and financial resources to this endeavour.

Vị linh thần thủ hộ tuổi Dần trong bộ Th: The guardian spirit of the Year of the Tiger in the Kim Hoàng Twelve Earthly Branches series. A mighty tiger-headed lord of the forest in a dragon robe, holding a guardian trident and standing on auspicious clouds, symbolizing supreme authority, steadfast courage, protection of the nation and people, and warding off evil from the home.
Vị linh thần thủ hộ tuổi Hợi trong bộ Th: The guardian spirit of the Year of the Pig in the Kim Hoàng Twelve Earthly Branches series. A general in fish-scale armor, brandishing a sword as he glides over golden clouds, symbolizing prosperity, abundant fortune, warmth and plenty, and a peaceful household.
Vị linh thần thủ hộ tuổi Mùi trong bộ Th: The guardian spirit of the Year of the Goat in the Kim Hoàng Twelve Earthly Branches series. A valiant goat-headed general drawing a sharp long sword, clad in gold-flecked armor and standing on auspicious clouds, symbolizing modesty with integrity, and the three rams heralding a new season of good omens and wealth.
Vị linh thần thủ hộ tuổi Sửu trong bộ Th: The guardian spirit of the Year of the Ox in the Kim Hoàng Twelve Earthly Branches series. A mighty ox-headed general holding a trident, one hand raised in salute to heaven and earth, symbolizing perseverance and diligence in building a livelihood, a thriving household and bountiful harvests.
Vị linh thần thủ hộ tuổi Thân trong bộ T: The guardian spirit of the Year of the Monkey in the Kim Hoàng Twelve Earthly Branches series. A majestic monkey spirit wielding a golden staff, clad in golden battle armor and riding auspicious clouds, symbolizing agile wisdom, strategic talent, banishing evil, and rising to honor and rank.
Vị linh thần thủ hộ tuổi Tuất trong bộ T: The guardian spirit of the Year of the Dog in the Kim Hoàng Twelve Earthly Branches series. A loyal dog-headed general gripping the hilt of a great sword, in guardian armor and riding auspicious clouds, symbolizing unwavering loyalty, driving away evil influences, and keeping the home peaceful and wealth lasting.
Vị linh thần thủ hộ tuổi Tỵ trong bộ Thậ: The guardian spirit of the Year of the Snake in the Kim Hoàng Twelve Earthly Branches series. A sacred serpent transformed into a majestic general, resting on a sapphire-blue sword and wearing a radiant five-color battle robe, symbolizing rebirth, adaptability, deep wisdom and lasting protection.
